items.title: The Upside-Down Moon
items.question: Capital letters H, I, N, O, S, X, and Z look the same upside down. How many letters of the word MOON survive being flipped?
items.correctExplanation: Three — both O's and the N survive rotation; only M breaks. Check each letter against the survivor list.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is 3. Test MOON letter by letter: M breaks, but O, O, and N all look identical upside down. Flipping words letter-by-letter beats guessing from the whole shape.
items.lessonContent:
Rotation symmetry hides in seven capital letters.
Test candidates one by one instead of judging wholes.
Lists of survivors turn flips into checklist work.
What breaks often matters more than what holds.
Share this: flip a word on paper and test each letter.

items.title: The Vowel Census
items.question: How many vowels (A, E, I, O, U) appear in the word BOOKKEEPER?
items.correctExplanation: Five — O, O, E, E, E. Walk the word left to right and tally; doubles count twice.
items.incorrectExplanation: Close — the answer is 5. March through BOOKKEEPER: B (no), O, O, K (no), K (no), E, E, P (no), E, R (no). Doubled vowels each count, giving O-O-E-E-E.
items.lessonContent:
Counting tasks reward left-to-right discipline.
Doubled letters count twice — never collapse them early.
Say each letter aloud to slow your eyes down.
Tallies beat impressions for every census task.
Share this: census the vowels in your own name.

items.title: The Third of Seven
items.question: Spell out the number 7 as a word. What is its third letter?
items.correctExplanation: V — S-E-V-E-N, and the third seat belongs to V. Spelling first, then indexing, is the whole method.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is V. Write SEVEN fully, then count seats: S is first, E is second, V is third. Two tiny steps in order beat one rushed guess.
items.lessonContent:
Index puzzles split into spell-then-count.
Number words are just letter strings in disguise.
Off-by-one errors die when you write positions down.
Slow two-step routines beat clever leaps.
Share this: ask someone for the fourth letter of ELEVEN.

items.title: The Midpoint Letter
items.question: A = 1, B = 2, C = 3, and so on. Which letter sits exactly halfway between B and H?
items.correctExplanation: E — B is 2, H is 8, and the midpoint 5 is E. Convert, average, convert back.
items.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is E. Number the letters (B = 2, H = 8), average to 5, and convert back to E. Alphabet math is just arithmetic wearing letters.
items.lessonContent:
Letters become numbers the moment you fix A at 1.
Midpoints need the average, not a guess between neighbors.
Convert there and back — never average the shapes.
Alphabet positions underlie codes, puzzles, and spreadsheets.
Share this: find the letter halfway between A and Z.

items.title: The Loyal Vowel
items.question: The word STRENGTHS is famous among word lovers. How many vowels does it contain?
items.correctExplanation: One — just the E hiding among eight consonants. Fame or not, count what is there.
items.incorrectExplanation: Close — the answer is 1. STRENGTHS carries a single E through nine letters, which is exactly its claim to fame. Length impresses; the census decides.
items.lessonContent:
Long words can carry almost no vowels at all.
Fame never changes a letter count — verify anyway.
Single-vowel giants reward the patient counter.
Check consonant clusters instead of assuming balance.
Share this: hunt the E hiding in STRENGTHS with a friend.

items.title: The Missing Seat
items.question: A, B, C, E, F, G — one letter is missing from this run. Which one?
items.correctExplanation: D — the run skips from C to E. Walk the alphabet alongside and the gap announces itself.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is D. Recite A through G beside the list: A, B, C match, then E appears where D should be. Gaps hide until you lay the full ruler down.
items.lessonContent:
Gap hunts need the complete ruler laid alongside.
Skips announce themselves only against full sequences.
Recite, don't scan — rhythm exposes breaks.
Missing-middle items hide better than missing ends.
Share this: delete one alphabet letter and time the hunt.

items.title: The Salesman Demo
items.question: TYPEWRITER is the longest common word typed using only a keyboard's top letter row. Verify it: which row does every one of its letters live on?
items.correctExplanation: Top — T, Y, P, E, W, R, I, T, E, R all sit on QWERTY's upper row. The machine's name was no accident.
items.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is top. Check each letter of TYPEWRITER against the keyboard: every one lives on the upper row. Salesmen allegedly typed it to prove the machine — legend or not, the letters check out.
items.lessonContent:
Keyboards are geography — words have addresses on them.
Verify letter claims against the actual rows.
Product names sometimes encode demonstrations.
Constraints (one row only) turn typing into puzzling.
Share this: find another word living on a single row.

items.title: The Left-Hand Parade
items.question: STEWARDESSES is the longest common word typed with the left hand alone on QWERTY. Count its letters to confirm the record length.
items.correctExplanation: Twelve letters, all left-hand keys. Count them: S-T-E-W-A-R-D-E-S-S-E-S. Records are just verified counts.
items.incorrectExplanation: Close — the answer is 12. Spell STEWARDESSES and tally: twelve seats, every one reachable by the left hand. Long-word records fall to anyone willing to count.
items.lessonContent:
Records are verified counts, not rumors.
Hand-zone maps turn keyboards into puzzle boards.
Longest-word hunts reward systematic trying.
Count first, marvel second.
Share this: find the longest right-hand-only word you can.

items.title: The Sweet Right Hand
items.question: LOLLIPOP is often cited as the longest word typed with only the right hand. How many letters does it hold?
items.correctExplanation: Eight — L-O-L-L-I-P-O-P, every key on the right side. Sweet and one-handed.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is 8. Count LOLLIPOP out: eight letters, all right-hand territory. Citations are starting points; your own count is the proof.
items.lessonContent:
Cite, then verify — even famous claims earn a recount.
Right-hand territory covers Y, U, I, O, P and below.
Short words can still hold records in tight categories.
Symmetry hunts (left versus right) organize the keyboard.
Share this: test whether LOLLIPOP obeys your own fingers.

items.title: The Mirrored Organ
items.question: What 3-letter body part reads exactly the same forward and backward?
items.correctExplanation: Eye — E-Y-E mirrors perfectly. The organ of reading reads the same both ways.
items.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is eye. Only one three-letter body part mirrors: E-Y-E. Palindrome hunting means testing reversals, and this one passes on sight.
items.lessonContent:
Palindromes read identically in both directions.
Test reversals mechanically — never trust the look.
Body parts hide neat wordplay (eye, noon-like pop).
Short words mirror most easily; start there.
Share this: find a palindrome longer than three letters.

items.title: The Scrambled Swimmer
items.question: Rearrange the letters C, I, F, A, I, P, C to name an ocean. What word do they spell?
items.correctExplanation: Pacific — P-A-C-I-F-I-C uses every tile exactly once. Count letters first, then hunt familiar shapes.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is Pacific. Arrange C-I-F-A-I-P-C into P-A-C-I-F-I-C and every tile is used once. Anagram solving means counting letters first, then hunting familiar shapes.
items.lessonContent:
Anagrams yield to letter counts before inspiration.
Count each letter's frequency, then match candidates.
Familiar proper nouns hide inside scrambled tiles.
Use every tile exactly once — leftovers mean retry.
Share this: scramble OCEAN and dare someone to Lakers it back.

items.title: The Stargazing Anagram
items.question: Rearrange ASTRONOMER to reveal what astronomers proverbially are. What two-word phrase appears?
items.correctExplanation: Moon starer — A-S-T-R-O-N-O-M-E-R reshuffles into M-O-O-N-S-T-A-R-E-R exactly. The profession describes itself.
items.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is moon starer. All ten letters of ASTRONOMER rebuild M-O-O-N S-T-A-R-E-R with none left over. Classic anagrams comment on their own subject — that self-reference is the confirmation signal.
items.lessonContent:
Self-describing anagrams confirm themselves by meaning.
Ten-letter shuffles need frequency counts, not staring.
Hyphens and spaces are free — only letters must balance.
Meaning-fit is the checksum after letter-fit.
Share this: anagram ASTRONOMER for someone and watch the grin.

items.title: The Ordered Vowels
items.question: What common word contains the vowels A, E, I, O, U in that exact order?
items.correctExplanation: Facetious — F-A-C-E-T-I-O-U-S lines all five vowels up in order. Order constraints make rare words findable.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is facetious. Walk it slowly: A, then E, then I, O, U — alphabetical vowels in sequence. Few words obey positional rules; those few are memorable.
items.lessonContent:
Positional rules (in order!) shrink huge searches fast.
Walk candidate words vowel by vowel.
Rare obedient words earn their fame honestly.
Constraints are searchlights, not obstacles.
Share this: challenge someone to beat FACETIOUS with another.

items.title: The Ghost's Census
items.question: The letters B and O both enclose space (B holds two pockets, O holds one). How many enclosed pockets appear in the word BOO?
items.correctExplanation: Four — B brings two, each O brings one: 2 + 1 + 1. Letters have architecture if you look.
items.incorrectExplanation: Close — the answer is 4. Score BOO piece by piece: B's two pockets plus one per O gives 2 + 1 + 1. Enclosed-space counting turns spelling into geometry.
items.lessonContent:
Letters have architecture: pockets, sticks, and curves.
Score words piece by piece, never by impression.
B counts double — its two pockets surprise everyone.
Geometry hides inside every spelled word.
Share this: score your name in pockets and sticks.

items.title: The Triple Mirror
items.question: What 4-letter time word reads the same forward, backward, and upside down?
items.correctExplanation: Noon — N-O-O-N mirrors forward-backward and survives rotation, since N and O both flip cleanly. Triple symmetry in four letters.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is noon. Check all three: forward NOON, backward NOON, upside-down NOON — N and O each survive the flip. Rare words pass every mirror you hold up.
items.lessonContent:
Stack symmetries: forward, backward, and rotated.
Test every claimed mirror mechanically.
N and O are the flipping elite — build from them.
Rare triple-passers earn their fame.
Share this: flip NOON on paper three ways.

items.title: The Calculator Greeting
items.question: Type 0.7734 on a calculator and turn it upside down. What greeting appears?
items.correctExplanation: Hello — 0.7734 flipped reads hELLO on seven-segment digits. Old calculators doubled as greeting cards.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is hello. Flip 0.7734 over: 4 becomes h, 3 becomes E, 7 becomes L, 7 becomes L, 0 becomes O. Segment digits were built for exactly this mischief.
items.lessonContent:
Seven-segment digits double as an upside-down alphabet.
Flip-and-read is a physical transformation, not a guess.
Constraints of display shape the possible words.
Old tech hid whole puzzle genres in its limits.
Share this: flip 0.7734 for someone with a calculator app.

items.title: The Neighbor Letter
items.question: In the alphabet, what single letter sits directly between J and L?
items.correctExplanation: K — J, K, L runs unbroken. Neighbors in sequences answer instantly when recited.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is K. Recite the stretch: J, then K, then L. Between-questions dissolve under direct recitation.
items.lessonContent:
Between-questions need recitation, not reasoning.
Say the sequence aloud and point at the middle.
Skipping ahead causes most off-by-one slips.
Anchor on known neighbors and step once.
Share this: ask for the letter between Q and S.

items.title: The Reversed Seven
items.question: Spell the word SEVEN backward, letter by letter. What string results?
items.correctExplanation: Neves — N-E-V-E-S reversed is S-E-V-E-N backwards... reversed letter by letter: S,E,V,E,N becomes N,E,V,E,S. Backward spelling is pure mechanics.
items.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is Neves. Write SEVEN, then read right to left: N, E, V, E, S. Reversal puzzles punish skippers and reward writers.
items.lessonContent:
Reversals demand writing, not mental flips.
Read right-to-left one seat at a time.
Palindromic middles (EVE here) anchor the work.
Mechanics beat memory for every backward task.
Share this: reverse your name and pronounce the result.

items.title: The Longest Month
items.question: Among the twelve month names, how many letters does the longest one hold?
items.correctExplanation: Nine — SEPTEMBER's nine letters top every month. Extremes fall to exhaustive comparison.
items.incorrectExplanation: Close — the answer is 9. Line the months up and measure: SEPTEMBER reaches nine, and nothing beats it. Superlative hunts need the full field, not the famous few.
items.lessonContent:
Superlatives need the whole field measured.
Famous candidates still require verification.
Count lengths, don't eyeball them.
Exhaustion is a legitimate solving method.
Share this: race someone to the longest weekday name.

items.title: The Midweek Syllables
items.question: Clap out the beats in WEDNESDAY. How many syllables does it carry?
items.correctExplanation: Two — WEDNES-day, two claps. Spelling suggests three, but the mouth knows better.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is 2. Clap it: WEDNES (one), DAY (two). Silent letters inflate the look; syllables follow sound, not spelling.
items.lessonContent:
Syllables follow sound, never spelling.
Clapping turns hearing into counting.
Silent letters inflate words visually.
Trust the mouth over the eye for beats.
Share this: clap WEDNESDAY for a doubter.

items.title: The Flipped Swimmer
items.question: What English word reads exactly the same when turned upside down?
items.correctExplanation: Swims — rotate S-W-I-M-S 180 degrees and it returns itself. Thematically perfect: it stays afloat either way.
items.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is swims. Flip each letter: S, W, I, M, S all survive rotation as a set, spelling SWIMS again. Whole-word flips need every letter to cooperate.
items.lessonContent:
Whole-word flips need unanimous letters.
Test the set, then test the order.
Meaning that matches the trick confirms the find.
Rotation words are a tiny elite club.
Share this: flip SWIMS on paper for a skeptic.

items.title: The Shortest Month
items.question: Which month name uses the fewest letters?
items.correctExplanation: May — three letters, shorter than every rival. Extremes at both ends fall to exhaustive comparison.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is May. Line the months up and measure: MAY reaches only three letters, beating June and July at four. Shortest-hunts need the same full field as longest-hunts.
items.lessonContent:
Minimums deserve the same full-field method as maximums.
Short famous answers still require verification.
Three-letter months are a club of one.
Pair longest with shortest for a complete picture.
Share this: race someone to the shortest weekday name.

items.title: The Self Question
items.question: How many letters spell the word ANSWER?
items.correctExplanation: Six — A-N-S-W-E-R runs six letters. The question answers itself if you count.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is 6. Spell ANSWER and tally: A, N, S, W, E, R — six. Self-referential questions still demand the mechanical count.
items.lessonContent:
Self-referential questions still need mechanical work.
Count the asker, not just the asked.
Six letters hiding in plain sight reward counters.
Never let cleverness skip the tally.
Share this: count the letters in QUESTION for a friend.

items.title: The Triple Double
items.question: What common word contains three pairs of consecutive doubled letters in a row?
items.correctExplanation: Bookkeeper — OO, KK, EE march consecutively through B-OO-KK-EE-PER. Triple doubles are vanishingly rare.
items.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is bookkeeper. Scan it slowly: OO, then KK, then EE — three doubled pairs back to back. Bookkeeping qualifies too, which is why both are accepted.
items.lessonContent:
Consecutive doubles are rare; triple runs nearly unique.
Scan slowly — doubles hide inside familiar words.
Accept near-twins when both satisfy the rule.
Rarity plus verifiability makes classics endure.
Share this: hunt the doubles in BOOKKEEPER aloud.

items.title: The Near-Alphabet
items.question: What common six-letter word has all of its letters in alphabetical order?
items.correctExplanation: Almost — A-L-M-O-S-T never steps backward. Six ordered letters in everyday clothing.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is almost. Walk A-L-M-O-S-T pair by pair: every step climbs. Ordinary words rarely file themselves so neatly.
items.lessonContent:
Order checks run pair by pair, never by glance.
Everyday words can hide perfect sequences.
Six ordered letters is the common-word ceiling.
Neatness in language rewards the checker.
Share this: test BEGIN for the same property.
